newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: MASS RALLY OF CONSTRUCTION WORKERS IN MELBOURNE

A mass rally of thousands of angry construction workers has ended in Melbourne, in a tense standoff with hundreds of police. Several scuffles broke out on the steps of Parliament House, where police estimate five thousand workers gathered to protest against government changes to Workcover.
Meanwhile, about 500 workers on the Citilink project have walked off the job indefinitely, following an accident this week where a young worker was trapped in a tunnel.
The construction union's secretary, Martin Kingham, says work on all sites will stop until there's a guarantee on work safety.
BEAZLEY "HAS NO CREDIBILITY" ON JOBS - HOWARD
Prime Minister, John Howard, has slammed Opposition claims that the Budget won't create jobs, saying Labor has no credibility on unemployment.
Mr Howard went on the offensive in Parliament, calling Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, Mr Eleven-point-two per cent unemployment, a reference to Mr Beazley's time as Employment Minister.
Mr Howard said Mr Beazley oversaw the highest rate of unemployment in Australia since the Great Depression, but still has the gall to attack the government.
The Opposition says the Budget does nothing for the jobless, and the Federation Fund is really a slush fund to target marginal seats.
FAHEY DEFENDS SAVINGS REBATE
Federal Finance Minister, John Fahey, says the tax rebate on interest earned on savings, announced in last night's Budget, will help reign in the current account deficit.
Mr Fahey has been forced to defend the move, which has been criticised by the Opposition and some economists on the grounds it doesn't do enough to encourage low and middle income earners.
The savings rebate, which will be capped at A$450 a year, has replaced the the former Labor Government's plan to contribute to people's superannuation savings.
Mr Fahey says the rebate will make people save more, but the extent of its success won't be evident until its full impact is felt in July 1999.
SOUTH AUSTRALIA DPP SAYS NITSCHKE CONFESSED TO MURDER
South Australia's Director of Public Prosecutions says he won't urge charges be laid against euthanasia advocate, Dr Phillip Nitschke, who he says has technically confessed to murder.
DPP Paul Rofe, who was attending a press club lunch where Dr Nitschke was speaking today, says the doctor made a technical confession by expressing an intent to end a patient's life.
During the speech Dr Nitschke described the circumstances of the death of terminally-ill patient, Esther Wild, following a coma, induced by an infusion of drugs.
Mr Rofe is, however, urging his Northern Territory counterpart not to prosecute Dr Nitschke, saying he doesn't believe a jury would convict him.
HOTELS AND MOTELS: TAKINGS UP, DEMAND LEVELLING OFF
A survey of the performance of Australia's hotels and motels has shown that Cairns, Melbourne, Perth and Sydney are bucking a national slowdown in the increase in demand for rooms.
But despite falling demand in other cities, the survey shows strong growth in gross takings.
The Hotel Watch survey shows a three-and-a-half per cent rise in room occupancy last year, well below the six per cent rise in 1995, reflecting slower growth in domestic tourism.
It shows the number of rooms available in the nation's 11 main cities and tourist destinations grew by five percent to 22.4 million.
In Cairns, Melbourne, Perth and Sydney, average occupancies exceeded 70 percent, underlining a need for additional rooms.
Gross takings from accommodation increased by almost 15 per cent to nearly A$2 billion.
KENNETT REFUSES TO DEBATE AG REPORT
The Victorian Government has refused to debate the latest report of the State Auditor General, who's stepped up his attack on proposed changes to his office.
Ches Baragawnath says the changes will render future parliament impotent in dealing with corrupt and oppresive governments.
He's accused the audit review panel of weakening his independence and questioning his integrity.
The Opposition Leader, John Brumby, has called for a parliamentary debate, or even an extra day's sitting, to examine the report.
But the Premier, Jeff Kennett, has refused, denying there's any threat to the auditor's independence.
IRC REPORTERS ANGRY AFTER BUDGET CUTS
Court reporters in the Australian Industrial Relations Commission may strike over a Federal Budget decision to hand their jobs to stenographers in the private sector.
The highly skilled members of the Auscript arm of the Attorney General's Department were told hours before yesterday's Budget release that their jobs were on the line.
The Australian Services Union, which represents the court reporters, have organised a national telephone hook-up for tomorrow to discuss the Budget move.
The Union's West Australian branch secretary, Margaret Dwyer, says tomorrow's conference will canvass new contracts for the workers to ensure their services are retained.
Ms Dwyer says industrial action can't be ruled out.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
